title: System Function
learningObjectives: Identify the structural roles of the rod and spacer tube.
student: Identify the primary structural function of the steel rod and aluminum tube assembly.
instructor: The steel rod carries the applied tensile load, while the aluminum tube acts as a compression spacer between the rigid collar and the fixed support. Together, they transfer load into the support and control the displacement of the free rod end.
gradingNotes: Students should recognize that this is a multi-member assembly and that both member deformations affect point C.

title: External Load and Supports
learningObjectives: Locate the applied load, restraint, and load-transfer interface.
student: Where is the external load applied, and where is the assembly supported or restrained?
instructor: The tensile load P is applied at the free rod end C. The assembly is supported at A by a rigid plate or wall. The rigid collar at B transfers load from the steel rod into the aluminum tube.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace the axial load through the rod, collar, tube, and support.
student: Trace the load path from the applied load to the fixed support.
instructor: The load acts on the steel rod at C. The rod carries it toward the rigid collar at B. The collar bears against the aluminum tube and places the tube in compression. The tube transfers the load to the fixed support at A.
commonMistakes: Do not treat the tube as unloaded merely because the applied force is placed on the rod.

title: Critical Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Identify displacement as the governing response for the supplied data.
student: What is the critical mechanical response to be evaluated in this problem?
instructor: The critical response is the axial displacement of point C relative to the fixed support at A. It depends on the elongation of the steel rod and the shortening of the aluminum tube.
gradingNotes: The base problem is deformation-focused because no material strength allowables are supplied.

title: Relevant Geometry and Material Properties
learningObjectives: Connect the controlling inputs to the axial-deformation equation.
student: Identify the geometric, material, and loading parameters that control the displacement response.
instructor: The controlling inputs are P, LAB, LBC, AAB, dBC or ABC, Eal, and Est. These enter the relation δ = NL/(AE).

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the physical assembly into a one-dimensional axial model.
student: Before using the reference figure, develop a simplified axial model of the assembly. Clearly identify the aluminum tube, steel rod, rigid collar, fixed support, and applied load.
instructor: A correct model represents two coaxial axial members: aluminum tube AB in compression and steel rod BC in tension, connected through a rigid collar at B, with a fixed support at A and load P at C.
gradingNotes: A clear one-dimensional model is sufficient; students do not need to reproduce the industrial geometry.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the axial deformation model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real assembly into the simplified mechanics model.
instructor: Typical assumptions are axial loading, a rigid collar, a fixed support at A, linear-elastic materials, small deformations, coaxial rod and tube, uniform member properties, and neglected local effects at threads, contacts, and the support opening.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the equilibrium and compatibility steps before calculation.
student: Explain how the displacement of C will be determined from the simplified model.
instructor: Determine the internal axial force in each member; compute rod elongation δC/B; compute tube shortening and interpret it as the displacement of B relative to A; then use δC/A = δB/A + δC/B.

title: Boundary Conditions and Member Action
learningObjectives: Interpret member action from the instructor reference idealization.
student: Using the instructor reference idealization, identify the boundary conditions and state which member is in tension and which member is in compression.
instructor: The support at A is fixed and load P is applied at C. Steel rod BC is in axial tension. Aluminum tube AB is in axial compression because collar B pushes against the tube as the rod is pulled.
commonMistakes: Assign tension or compression from the physical load path, not only from the visual direction of the applied arrow.

title: Internal Axial Forces
learningObjectives: Determine member axial forces and classify their signs.
student: For P = {{P}} {{P_unit}}, determine the internal axial force in steel rod BC and aluminum tube AB. Use tension as positive.
instructor: Equilibrium and the load path give NBC = +{{axial_force_BC_kN}} kN in tension and NAB = {{axial_force_AB_kN}} kN in compression.
gradingNotes: Equivalent sign conventions are acceptable when the physical tension/compression classifications and magnitudes are correct.

title: Steel Rod Elongation
learningObjectives: Calculate rod area and axial elongation with consistent units.
student: Calculate the elongation of steel rod segment BC. First determine its area from dBC = {{d_BC}} {{d_BC_unit}}.
instructor:
ABC = π({{d_BC}} mm)2/4 = {{axial_area_BC_mm2}} mm2. With Est = {{E_st}} GPa = {{axial_E_st_MPa}} N/mm2,

δC/B = NBCLBC/(ABCEst) = {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm to the right.
commonMistakes: Convert kN to N and GPa to N/mm2 when lengths and areas are in millimeters.

title: Aluminum Tube Shortening and Displacement of B
learningObjectives: Calculate compressive shortening and interpret point displacement.
student: Calculate the axial shortening of aluminum tube AB and interpret it as the displacement of point B relative to fixed point A.
instructor:
The tube carries {{P}} kN in compression. Its shortening magnitude is

|δB/A| = |NAB|LAB/(AABEal) = {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm.

Because the tube shortens while A remains fixed, collar point B moves {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm to the right relative to A.
commonMistakes: A negative compressive strain does not mean B moves left. Relate the shortening to the fixed end A and the actual member geometry.

title: Total Displacement of C
learningObjectives: Combine relative member deformations into the displacement of a point.
student: Determine the total displacement of end C relative to fixed support A. Show the displacement-compatibility relation and state the direction.
instructor:
Both contributions move C to the right:

δC/A = δB/A + δC/B = {{axial_tube_shortening_mm}} mm + {{axial_rod_elongation_mm}} mm = {{axial_total_displacement_mm}} mm to the right.
gradingNotes: Require students to show why the deformation magnitudes add instead of relying only on a memorized sign rule.

title: Engineering Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain the physical meaning and direction of the combined displacement.
student: Explain why the rod elongation and tube shortening contribute to the displacement of C in the same direction. Briefly state what the result means for a component positioned or preloaded by end C.
instructor: The steel rod elongates under tension, moving C to the right relative to B. Simultaneously, the aluminum tube shortens and allows collar B to move right relative to fixed support A. The motions therefore add. For the assigned data, C moves {{axial_total_displacement_mm}} mm to the right, which is the position or preload-setting displacement that the connected component would experience in this idealized elastic model.
